title: Duties 5–6: professional & inclusive practice
blurb: Working as an accountable professional within your scope, handling complaints, supporting informed decisions, and giving fair, inclusive care.
question: The assessor asks: "Tell me about a time you were asked to do something you weren't sure you should do, and how you make sure every patient gets fair care." Which standards, laws and boundaries should your answer show?

teach.body: Duty 5 is to "practise as an autonomous professional exercising judgement and integrity, keeping within the scope of practice and the legal and ethical boundaries of the profession". Autonomous means you own your decisions and actions. Even when you follow a dentist's direction, you are personally accountable to your patients, the GDC, your team and the public. That's why the GDC Scope of Practice says you must only carry out tasks you are trained, competent and indemnified (or insured) to do.

teach.h: Asked to do a task: should you?

root.label: Is it within a dental nurse's scope?

children.label: Carry it out and record it

teach.caption: The GDC says a dental nurse who doesn't feel trained or competent for a task should not be pressured to accept it.

head: Principle
rows: Have a clear and effective complaints procedure
Work with colleagues in patients' best interests
Maintain, develop and work within your knowledge and skills
Raise concerns if patients are at risk
Personal behaviour maintains confidence in you and the profession
teach.caption: Upholding these is one of the behaviours expected across every duty. The GDC has consulted on replacing them, so check for updates.

teach.body: Valid consent is given voluntarily by a patient who has capacity and has been properly informed about the options, risks, benefits and costs, including doing nothing. It can be withdrawn at any time. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, adults are assumed to have capacity unless shown otherwise. Your part: help the patient understand, never pressure them, and tell the dentist if a patient seems unsure or changes their mind.

teach.h: When a patient complains to you
items: Listen without interrupting, and take them somewhere private if you can.
Stay calm and polite; don't argue or become defensive.
Acknowledge their feelings and say you're sorry they've had a poor experience.
Explain the practice complaints procedure and who will handle it.
Record what was said and pass it promptly to the complaints lead.
If something went wrong, be open and honest about it (duty of candour).

teach.body: Duty 6 is to "practise in a non-discriminatory and inclusive manner recognising the impact of culture, equality and diversity". In England, Scotland and Wales the Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics; Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. Inclusion goes beyond not discriminating. It means making reasonable adjustments, showing cultural competence, and challenging discriminatory language and microaggressions, whether from colleagues, patients or other professionals.

teach.caption: Equal outcomes sometimes need different arrangements. That's what reasonable adjustments are for.

teach.text: "Autonomous" doesn't mean working without the dentist or doing tasks on your own initiative. Dental nurses still work under prescription, direction or delegation. It means taking personal responsibility for your own judgement and actions, including saying no when something is outside your scope or competence.

items: Duty 5: accountable professional, within scope, law and ethics; trained, competent and indemnified.
Know the GDC's nine principles and use them to justify your actions.
Valid consent: voluntary, informed, with capacity; tell the dentist if a patient is unsure.
Complaints: listen, stay calm, explain the procedure, record, pass to the lead, be candid.
Duty 6: nine protected characteristics, reasonable adjustments, challenge discrimination.

summary: You can now explain what acting as an accountable professional means for a dental nurse, decide whether to accept a task, name the GDC's nine principles, describe your part in consent and complaints, and show how you give fair, inclusive care with reasonable adjustments and by challenging discrimination.

A.q: The dentist asks you to apply fluoride varnish to a child, but you have never been trained to do it. What should you do?
options: Do it, as the dentist has prescribed it
Do it, but ask the dentist to watch you
Explain you aren't trained and decline for now
Ask the child's parent if they mind you trying
A.why: Fluoride varnish on prescription is an additional skill. You must be trained, competent and indemnified first, and you should not be pressured into it.

whyNot.0: A prescription doesn't make you trained or competent to carry it out.
whyNot.1: Being watched isn't a substitute for proper training.
whyNot.3: A parent's agreement doesn't make an untrained task safe or within your competence.

A.q: Which GDC principle requires a practice to have a clear and effective complaints procedure?
options: Principle 1
Principle 5
Principle 7
Principle 9
A.why: Principle 5 is "Have a clear and effective complaints procedure".

whyNot.0: Principle 1 is putting patients' interests first.
whyNot.2: Principle 7 is maintaining and working within your knowledge and skills.
whyNot.3: Principle 9 is personal behaviour that maintains confidence in the profession.

A.q: A patient complains angrily to you at reception about a long wait. What is the best first response?
options: Tell him the dentist is busy and he must be patient
Explain it isn't your fault and walk away
Ask him to put his complaint in an email to the practice later
Listen calmly, acknowledge it and explain the procedure
A.why: Listening calmly, acknowledging how he feels and explaining how complaints are handled is the professional first response.

whyNot.0: Dismissing the complaint is likely to make things worse.
whyNot.1: Being defensive and walking away isn't professional.
whyNot.2: Patients can complain verbally; it should be recorded and passed on, not pushed back.

B.q: What does "practise as an autonomous professional" mean for a dental nurse?
options: Taking personal responsibility for your own judgement
Carrying out treatment without a dentist present in the room
Choosing your own patients and appointment times
Following every instruction without question
B.why: Autonomy means owning your decisions and actions and being accountable for them, while still working within scope and under direction.

whyNot.1: Dental nurses work under prescription, direction or delegation; they don't treat independently.
whyNot.2: Autonomy isn't about choosing patients or hours.
whyNot.3: Accountability means you must question or decline unsafe or out-of-scope instructions.

B.q: For consent to be valid, which conditions must be met?
options: Signed in writing, dated and witnessed
Given by the patient's next of kin
Voluntary, informed and with capacity
Obtained at the patient's first visit only
B.why: Valid consent is given voluntarily by a patient with capacity who has been properly informed.

whyNot.0: Written consent can be useful, but a signature alone doesn't make consent valid.
whyNot.1: Adults with capacity give their own consent; next of kin can't consent for them.
whyNot.3: Consent is ongoing and is needed for each treatment; it can be withdrawn.

B.q: A patient who uses a wheelchair has been booked into your first-floor surgery, and there is no lift. What is the inclusive action?
options: Ask her to try to manage the stairs with help
Rebook her into a ground-floor surgery
Treat her in the waiting room instead
Refer her elsewhere as you can't help
B.why: Moving the appointment to an accessible surgery is a reasonable adjustment that gives her equal access to care.

whyNot.2: The waiting room isn't a clinical area and lacks equipment, privacy and infection control.
whyNot.3: Refusing care when a reasonable adjustment is available would be discriminatory.

C.q: A colleague mocks a patient's accent after he leaves the surgery. What should you do?
options: Laugh along, as the patient didn't hear it
Ignore it, as it isn't your business
Post about it anonymously online
Challenge it calmly and professionally
C.why: Dental nurses should proactively address discriminatory language and microaggressions, including from colleagues. Escalate if it continues.

whyNot.0: Joining in condones discrimination, whether the patient heard it or not.
whyNot.1: Inclusive practice includes speaking up when you see discrimination.
whyNot.2: Discussing colleagues or patients online breaches professional standards.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
options: Religion or belief
Income level
Pregnancy and maternity
Sexual orientation
C.why: Income isn't one of the nine protected characteristics, though it can still affect access to care.

C.q: After the dentist explains an extraction, the patient quietly says, "I suppose so," and looks worried. What is your role?
options: Let the dentist know she seems unsure
Reassure her that it will be fine and carry on
Answer her clinical questions about the risks
Ask her to sign the form quickly before she changes her mind
C.why: If a patient seems unsure, consent may not be properly informed or voluntary. Telling the dentist lets them explain further before treatment.

whyNot.1: False reassurance doesn't make consent valid.
whyNot.2: Explaining clinical risks of the procedure is the dentist's role.
whyNot.3: Rushing a patient to sign is pressure, which makes consent invalid.

reteach.title: A licence with conditions
reteach.question: What does your GDC registration actually allow you to do, and what does it ask of you?

blocks.body: Registration is a bit like a licence. It lets you work as a dental nurse, but only within its conditions: your scope of practice, the things you're trained and competent in, and the GDC's standards. Inside those lines you use your own judgement and you answer for it personally. And the licence applies to every patient equally, which is why fair, inclusive care is part of the deal, not an extra.

blocks.text: Saying "the dentist told me to" is not a defence if a task was outside your scope or competence. You are accountable for your own actions.

explain.body: Only carry out tasks within a dental nurse's scope that you are trained, competent and indemnified for. If not, say so and ask for training. You shouldn't be pressured to accept.

test.q: According to the GDC, which three things must apply before you carry out any task?
options: Paid, insured and supervised
Trained, competent and indemnified
Qualified, experienced and rostered
Requested, recorded and consented
test.why: The GDC says you must only carry out tasks you are trained, competent and indemnified (or insured) to do.

whyNot.0: Being paid or supervised isn't the GDC test.
whyNot.2: Experience and rotas don't replace training and competence.
whyNot.3: Recording and consent matter, but the GDC's test is trained, competent and indemnified.

explain.body: They set the standards every registrant must meet. Use them to explain why you acted as you did: for example, principle 4 for confidentiality or principle 8 for raising a concern.

test.q: Which GDC principle is "Put patients' interests first"?
options: Principle 6
Principle 4
Principle 9
Principle 1

whyNot.0: Principle 6 is working with colleagues in patients' best interests.
whyNot.2: Principle 9 is personal behaviour maintaining confidence.

explain.body: Consent must be voluntary, informed and given with capacity; tell the dentist if a patient is unsure. With complaints, listen, stay calm, explain the procedure, record it and pass it on.

test.q: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what must you assume about an adult patient?
options: They lack capacity until a doctor confirms it
They have capacity unless shown otherwise
They need a relative present to consent
They lack capacity if they choose unwisely
test.why: The Act says a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it.

whyNot.0: The starting point is the opposite: capacity is assumed.
whyNot.2: Adults with capacity consent for themselves.
whyNot.3: The Act says an unwise decision alone doesn't mean someone lacks capacity.

explain.body: Nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. Make reasonable adjustments, show cultural competence and challenge discrimination and microaggressions.

test.q: An autistic patient finds the busy waiting room distressing. Which is a reasonable adjustment?
options: Ask him to sit facing the wall in the waiting room
Tell him the waiting room is the same for everyone
Offer a quiet first appointment of the day
Refer him to another practice
test.why: A quiet first appointment reduces distress and gives him equal access, which is a reasonable adjustment.

whyNot.0: He would still be in the busy room, so the cause of his distress is unchanged.
whyNot.1: Treating everyone the same can be unfair when needs differ.
whyNot.3: Referring away avoids the duty to adjust.
